title: Contains Duplicate
keyIdea: Remember what you've already seen. A hash set answers "have I met this number before?" in O(1) on average, so one pass over the array is enough. Check first, then insert.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Compare every pair (i, j) with i < j. If any two are equal, return true.
approaches.why: About n·(n−1)/2 pairs. With n up to 10⁵ that's ~5·10⁹ comparisons, too slow.

approaches.name: Sort, then check neighbours
approaches.idea: After sorting, equal numbers sit next to each other, so one pass comparing nums[i] with nums[i-1] finds any repeat.
approaches.why: Sorting costs O(n log n); the scan after it is O(n). No extra container (std::sort uses O(log n) stack).
approaches.warn: Changes the order of nums. Fine here, but say it out loud in an interview.

approaches.name: Hash set
approaches.idea: Walk the array once. For each number, ask the set if it's already there: yes → return true. No → insert it and keep going.
approaches.why: n numbers, each with one count() and at most one insert(), both O(1) on average. The set can grow to n numbers.

quiz.q: Why does the code call seen.count(num) before seen.insert(num)?
options: If it inserted first, count would always find the number it just added and every array would look like it has a duplicate
insert would crash on a duplicate

quiz.q: Why is seen.count(num) O(1) on average?
options: The set only looks in the one bucket that num hashes to, not at every stored number
It stops after the first element

quiz.q: What does the hash set approach trade for its O(n) time?
options: O(n) extra memory for the set
It only works on positive numbers

quiz.q: You can't use extra memory but may change the array. Best option?
options: Sort, then compare neighbours: O(n log n), O(1) extra
Brute force is the only way

steps: How big can the array get? Can you change it? Do you need to say which number repeats?
Try [1,2,3,1] and [1,2,3,4]. When can you stop early?
Every pair: time? Sorting first: time, and what does it change?
"Have I seen this before?": which container answers that in O(1)?
Check before insert, or insert before check? Why does the order matter?
Code the one pass with seen.count and seen.insert.
Dry-run [1,2,3,1]: what's in seen when i = 3?
Time and space? How would LC 219 (repeat within distance k) change it?
